Staff. This Reply Brief will address certain of the arguments set out by other parties. There is of

the scope of its Reply Brief to those arguments necessary to present the essence of its case.

       the need for this project. Simply put, the demand projections the Applicants cite again and

       again may justify two Import Paths to the Permian Basin, but do not justify three. Import

    B. Two Lines Are Sufficient for Non-Large-Load Demand Through 2038.

        7.       Each line of this project has a rated capacity of 7,131 MVA. 8 Using the power factor

incremental difference of 6,214 MW is well within the capacity of a single line.

        8.       The PBRP’s outage assumption is “loss of single generating unit, transmission

circuit, transformer, or common tower outage.” 10 Under the N-1 standard, as long as each line

individually covers the incremental non-large-load demand, one line can be out without requiring

the non-765-kV system to carry the increment. Therefore, two lines comfortably cover oil and gas

and non-large load demands in the region through 2038.

        9.       More precisely, the incremental oil and gas plus all other non-large-load need in the

support the raw non-large-load forecasted numbers independently. Therefore, the question is how

much weight to assign large-load forecasts, and whether ratepayers should be burdened to fund

VI.        REPLY REGARDING STATE PARKS.

           38.     The Legislature expressly directed that the effects on State Parks should be taken

into account when routing transmission lines. 38

           39.     The State Park System exists to preserve and steward natural, scenic, cultural, and

historic resources of statewide significance while providing resource-oriented public recreation for

present and future generations. That policy is reflected in Parks & Wildlife Code Chapter 13,

Chapter 26, and the Parks & Wildlife Commission’s land-classification rules in 31 Tex. Admin.

Code § 59.64.

           40.     The Texas State Park System exists to preserve, steward, and interpret natural,

scenic, cultural, and historic resources of statewide significance while providing opportunities for

resource-oriented public recreation and education for present and future generations. The value of

a state park is not limited to the acreage within its surveyed boundaries. Rather, many of the natural,

scenic, cultural, and recreational values for which a park is established derive from the broader

landscape in which the park is situated. Scenic vistas, undeveloped horizons, wildlife habitat,

ecological connectivity, dark skies, quiet soundscapes, historic settings, and the visual character of

the surrounding environment often constitute integral components of the park experience and of

 the resources the park was created to protect.

       41.     Accordingly, effective stewardship of a state park necessarily includes

consideration of external activities that may substantially alter or degrade those surrounding

conditions. While the State’s direct management authority may be limited to lands within park

boundaries, the conservation objectives reflected in Parks and Wildlife Code Chapters 13 and 26

and in the Commission’s land-classification rules recognize that preservation of park resources is

not merely a matter of protecting a surveyed tract of land. It also requires, where reasonably

possible, protecting the environmental, scenic, and cultural context that gives those resources their

meaning and value.

       42.     The public’s interest in a state park therefore extends beyond protection of discrete

natural features located within the park itself. Visitors come to experience landscapes, viewsheds,

ecosystems, historical settings, and recreational opportunities that frequently depend upon

conditions existing both inside and outside park boundaries. Actions that materially impair those

surrounding conditions may diminish the very resources that the State Park System was established

to conserve and present to the public.

       43.     For that reason, preservation of the Texas State Park System is most faithfully

understood as preservation not only of park lands themselves, but also—when feasible and

consistent with governing law—of the scenic, ecological, cultural, and historical setting that

contributes to the parks’ long-term character, integrity, and public value.

       44.     Here, applying that framework to this case leads to one clear choice: the River

should be crossed via link U3 to lessen impacts on both the Colorado River and the State Park

System.

        38.      The Legislature expressly directed that the effects on State Parks should be taken

into account when routing transmission lines.38

        39.      The State Park System exists to preserve and steward natural, scenic, cultural, and

historic resources of statewide significance while providing resource-oriented public recreation for

present and future generations. That policy is reflected in Parks & Wildlife Code Chapter 13,

Chapter 26, and the Parks & Wildlife Commission's land-classification rules in 31 Tex. Admin.

Code § 59.64.

        40.      The Texas State Park System exists to preserve, steward, and interpret natural,

scenic, cultural, and historic resources of statewide significance while providing opportunities for

resource-oriented public recreation and education for present and future generations. The value of

a state park is not limited to the acreage within its surveyed boundaries. Rather, many ofthe natural,

scenic, cultural, and recreational values for which a park is established derive from the broader

landscape in which the park is situated. Scenic vistas, undeveloped horizons, wildlife habitat,

ecological connectivity, dark skies, quiet soundscapes, historic settings, and the visual character of

the surrounding environment often constitute integral components of the park experience and of

       41.     Accordingly,    effective   stewardship   of a state park necessarily includes

consideration of external activities that may substantially alter or degrade those surrounding

conditions. While the State's direct management authority may be limited to lands within park

boundaries, the conservation obj ectives reflected in Parks and Wildli fe Code Chapters 13 and 26

and in the Commission's land-classification rules recognize that preservation of park resources is

not merely a matter of protecting a surveyed tract of land. It also requires, where reasonably

possible, protecting the environmental, scenic, and cultural context that gives those resources their

meaning and value.

       42.     The public's interest in a state park therefore extends beyond protection of discrete

natural features located within the park itself. Visitors come to experience landscapes, viewsheds,

ecosystems, historical settings, and recreational opportunities that frequently depend upon

conditions existing both inside and outside park boundaries. Actions that materially impair those

surrounding conditions may diminish the very resources that the State Park System was established

to conserve and present to the public.

       43.     For that reason, preservation of the Texas State Park System is most faithfully

understood as preservation not only of park lands themselves, but also-when feasible and

consistent with governing law-of the scenic, ecological, cultural, and historical setting that

contributes to the parks' long-term character, integrity, and public value.
